issues.legal_issue: An unpaid purchase-price obligation does not qualify as a loan merely because payment is deferred in instalments with interest, where the parties have not converted the obligation into a loan.
material_facts: The purchasers owed the seller the price for property under an agreement of sale.
A compromise decree provided that the property would belong to a purchaser and charged it with the unpaid purchase money.
The decree allowed payment of the amount due in instalments with interest.
There was no evidence that the parties agreed to treat the unpaid purchase price as a loan or otherwise changed its character.
The purchasers sought protection and a refund under the statutory limit on amounts recoverable from borrowers, although they had paid more than twice the amount stated as the original purchase price.
issues.conclusion: The unpaid purchase price remained a purchase-price obligation and was not a loan. The purchasers were not borrowers entitled to statutory relief, so their appeal was dismissed and the claimed relief was unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(2), 2(12) and 30 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, relief under Section 30 requires that the person be a borrower and that the amount payable be in respect of a loan. A loan includes an advance repayable with interest and a transaction that is in substance a loan; an actual advance is not invariably necessary, but the substance of the transaction must show that the obligation was treated as a loan. A debt is not necessarily a loan. Deferring unpaid purchase money in instalments and charging interest does not, without more, change its character. The Court distinguished Fateh Chand Mahesri v. Akimuddin Chaudhury, where the parties’ treatment of the purchase price as paid off and the amount as a loan was evidenced, and Nirode Barani Debya v. Sisir Kumar Mukherjee, which likewise involved the purchase-price obligation being treated as discharged and replaced by a loan. The continued character of an unpaid vendor’s purchase-money claim is consistent with the charge described in Section 55(4)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act.

rule.if: statutory_borrower_relief_claim and obligation_is_unpaid_purchase_price and property_conveyed_to_purchaser and seller_has_charge_for_unpaid_price and payment_only_deferred_with_interest and not obligation_converted_into_loan

predicates.statutory_borrower_relief_claim: A person claims statutory relief on the basis that an amount demanded from them is payable as a borrower.
predicates.obligation_is_unpaid_purchase_price: The amount demanded arose as purchase money that remained unpaid for property sold to the person liable to pay it.
predicates.property_conveyed_to_purchaser: The seller conveyed the property to the purchaser while some purchase money remained unpaid.
predicates.seller_has_charge_for_unpaid_price: The seller retained or received a charge over the property to secure the unpaid purchase money.
predicates.payment_only_deferred_with_interest: The parties allowed the unpaid purchase money to be paid later, including by instalments, with interest.
predicates.obligation_converted_into_loan: The parties agreed or otherwise treated the unpaid purchase-price obligation as discharged and replaced by a loan obligation.

issues.definition: When a person seeks borrower relief for unpaid purchase money, the property has been conveyed, the seller has security for the unpaid price, payment was only deferred with interest, and the obligation was not converted into a loan, the rule makes borrower relief unavailable.
